Your application project most likely contains files, such as tables, that users need to modify. However, when you build an application from a [[T0]] project, the files in the project are assembled into a single application file, and the files in the project that are designated as included become read-only.

For files that users need to modify, you should add them to your project but exclude them from the build process. Excluded files remain part of your application, so [[T1]] continues to track them as part of your project. However, excluded files are not compiled into the application file so users can modify them.

Generally, you should include executable files, such as forms, reports, queries, menus, and programs, and all other files that users do not need to update. You should exclude data files, ActiveX control (.ocx) libraries, [[T2]] dynamic-link libraries (.fll), and Windows dynamic-link libraries (.dll). By default, tables are excluded because it is assumed that users change tables in an application.

> **Note:** You cannot include application (.app) files in a project. You cannot exclude files that are designated as main files. For more information about main files, see How to: Set the Starting Point .

However, you should include or exclude files based on your application requirements. For example, you might include a table that contains sensitive system information or read-only information to protect it from inadvertent changes. Conversely, if your application permits users to change a report, you might exclude the report.

When [[T0]] starts, you can specify a configuration file or bypass all configuration files, allowing [[T1]] to use its default settings.

When [[T2]] loads a configuration file, the settings in that file take precedence over corresponding default settings made in the Options dialog box.

- In the command line that starts [[T0]], specify the -C switch and the name of the configuration file that you want to use (including a path if necessary). Do not put a space between the switch and the file name. -or-
- In Windows, double-click the name of the configuration file to use. [[T1]] will start using the configuration file you have selected.

If you want to avoid using any configuration file, including the default file [[T2]], you can suppress all configuration files. This causes [[T3]] to use only the default settings established in the Options dialog box.

- In the command line that starts [[T0]], add the -C switch with nothing after it. For example, to avoid any configuration file found in the startup directory or the system path, use this command line: [[T1]] VersionNumber .exe -C

You can use an external configuration file in addition to an internal configuration file in circumstances where you need to configure settings separately. For example, setting [[I0]] should be performed in an internal configuration file.

You can set [[T0]] to read an external configuration file following an internal configuration file by using the new [[T1]] directive in the internal configuration file. When you include the setting [[I1]] in the internal configuration file, [[T2]] searches for an external configuration file, usually [[T3]], and reads its settings. You can also specify a different configuration file using the [[I2]] command-line switch when starting [[T4]].

> **Note:** For .exe and .dll file servers, [[T5]] supports only those configuration files bound inside the server. Therefore, [[T6]] disregards the [[T7]] setting.

- In the internal configuration file, set the special term [[T0]] to on. [[T1]] = [[T2]]
- When you start your program, either specify a second configuration file using the -C command-line switch or have a second configuration file in the default program path.

For more information about command-line switches, see How to: Use Command-Line Options When Starting [[T3]].

The settings in an external configuration file take precedence over those in the internal configuration file, if duplicate settings exist, because the external configuration file is read after the internal file. [[T4]] does not begin initialization until it reads both files.

If you want to specify the configuration file as read-only, place the file in your project and mark it as Included. | Topic Name | A name that specifies a logical set of data. For file-based applications, topic names are usually file names. In other applications, topic names are application-specific. To access the server, the client must specify a topic name in addition to the server's service name. |
| Item Name | A name that specifies a unit of data that the server can pass to the client requesting the data. |
